newsitem.title: USA: FDR angered by Swiss bankers in war, document says.
newsitem.headline: FDR angered by Swiss bankers in war, document says.

text.p: President Franklin Roosevelt was so angry that Swiss bankers were buying Nazi gold in 1944 that he ordered action "to block Swiss participation in saving the skins of rich or prominent Germans," according to a secret Second World War document released on Friday.

Roosevelt was reacting to a secret July 10, 1944 report from U.S. intelligence chief William "Wild Bill" Donovan that despite demands by the United States and Britain that the Swiss halt gold transactions with the Germans, the Swiss National Bank had made a secret deal to buy up to 6,000 kilograms (13,230 lb) of German gold a month in 1944.

Donovan, the head of the Office of Strategic Services, the forerunner of the CIA, said in a secret memorandum to the president that the OSS's agent in Berne reported that "under the fairly broad arrangement ... it will be possible to exchange Swiss francs just as before ..."

The Berne agent, Allan Dulles, who later became the CIA's director, also reported that the Germans were able under this arrangement to meet their foreign exchange requirements and to buy millions of dollars worth of ball bearings for their defense effort.

Roosevelt ordered Dovovan to take the matter up with the U.S. Secretary of State "right away," and he added, "We ought to block the Swiss participation in saving the skins of rich or prominent Nazis."

The document was unearthed this week by researchers for the World Jewish Congress, which is combing the U.S. National Archives trying to find documents relating to the assets of Holocaust victims that were deposited in Swiss banks.
The United States and Britain held a secret meeting with the Swiss in Lisbon, Portugal, in 1944 to demand restrictions on Swiss bank dealings with the Germans.
